name: Excalibur
powers: Blade that cut through any armor; scabbard protected the wearer from wounding.
description: The great sword of King Arthur, given to him by the Lady of the Lake and returned to her waters after his death at Camlann. In Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur its scabbard protects the wearer from wounding. The name also attaches to the sword Arthur drew from the stone in later romance.

name: Eye of Horus
powers: Protects the wearer and restores wholeness; the healed eye of the falcon god.
description: The wedjat, the eye that the god Thoth healed after Set tore it from Horus, worn as an amulet of protection, healing, and wholeness. Its hieroglyphic fractions were used for measuring grain volumes, and thousands of wedjat amulets in faience, gold, and stone survive in tombs from the Old Kingdom into the Graeco-Roman period, where the sign still guarded the living and the dead.
source: Egyptian amulets and temple reliefs; Pyramid Texts

name: Elixir of Immortality
description: The drug of immortality that Hou Yi obtained from the Queen Mother of the West. His wife Chang'e swallowed it to keep it from a thief and drifted to the moon, where she lives forever in the cold lunar palace with the jade rabbit; the tale, recorded in Han-era sources, gave the moon its goddess and the Mid-Autumn Festival its story.

name: The Emerald Buddha's Robes
aliases: Royal Vestments of the Emerald Buddha
description: The three robes of gold worn by the Emerald Buddha in the Wat Phra Kaew temple in Bangkok and changed at the turn of each season in a ceremony performed by the king. The jeweled garments, their alternation fixed by royal ritual, mark the image as the palladium of the Thai state and the axis of the kingdom's legitimacy.

name: Ehecailacacozcatl
powers: Command of the wind that sweeps the road before the rain gods.
description: The shell breast ornament of the wind god Quetzalcoatl, a spiral conch called ehecailacacozcatl ('wind jewel') worn at the throat and tied to the whirlwind that scatters rain and seeds. Aztec images of Quetzalcoatl-Ehecatl show the spiral shell, sometimes a cut conch worn as a pectoral, among his emblems; colonial texts connect it to his journeys sweeping the road before Tlaloc's rain.

name: Eleke
material: Beaded necklaces in the colors of the orishas
era: Cuban Santería tradition to the present
powers: Binds the wearer to the protection of a specific orisha.
description: The bead necklaces of Cuban Santería, each strung in the colors of a particular orisha and given in ceremony to mark the wearer under that spirit's protection. The eleke is consecrated and must be removed only with respect, and its colors reveal the orisha to those who know the tradition. It descends from the beaded collars of Yoruba religion and marks initiation and devotion.
source: Cuban Santería practice and ethnographic studies

name: Edan Ogboni Staff
era: Traditional, still used in society rites
powers: Held to enforce truth and justice, sealing oaths made before the earth's authority.
description: The edan are paired brass or iron staffs of the Yoruba Ogboni (Osugbo) society, each topped by a seated human figure joined by a chain. The male-female pair stands for the moral unity of the earth and is kept on the society's altar, where oaths were sworn over it. It symbolises truth, justice, and the moral authority of the elders of the earth.
source: Ogboni society tradition; British Museum collections

name: Ethiopian Processional Cross
description: Ethiopian processional crosses are tall brass or silver crosses with a lattice of openwork tracery, carried on a staff before the clergy in Ethiopian Orthodox liturgy. Each cross is unique, and their intricate patterns symbolise the Tree of Life and the victory of Christ; the cross is held to carry divine protection over the faithful.

name: Ethiopian Ketab Protective Scroll
material: Parchment, ink, leather or cloth cover
powers: Worn or hung to ward off evil spirits, illness, and the harm attributed to buda.
description: Ketab are protective prayer scrolls of the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition, parchment strips inscribed with prayers, names, and devotional images, rolled and worn or hung as amulets. Written by debtera (church scholars) and diviners, they guard against evil spirits, illness, and the harm believed to come from buda. Their style ranges from simple folded slips to elaborate illustrated rolls.
source: Ethiopian magical scroll tradition; scholarly studies (J. Mercier)

name: Ancient Egyptian Kohl Tube
description: Ancient Egyptian kohl tubes are slender cosmetic containers, often of wood, stone, or faience, used to hold kohl eye-paint. Applied with a stick, kohl protected the eyes from sun and flies and carried religious meaning, its dark-lined eye echoing the apotropaic gaze of Horus; fine decorated examples survive from the New Kingdom.
source: Museum collections (British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art)

name: Ektara
description: One-stringed lute of rural Bengal, a gourd or bamboo body with a single steel string struck and plucked, carried by wandering Baul singers. The ektara's thin drone accompanies the mystic songs of the Bauls of Bengal, and the instrument is bound to the oral tradition of the region's wandering bards, who sing of the divine within the human body.

name: Eglė's Dress
description: In the Lithuanian tale 'Eglė the Queen of Serpents', the clothes Eglė wore when bathing at the lake — a coiled grass snake slipped into her sleeve and would return her clothing only if she promised to marry its king. That pledged garment drives the tale: nine years under the sea, three impossible tasks, and Eglė's lasting transformation into a spruce tree.
source: Lithuanian folk tale 'Eglė žalčių karalienė'; first translation printed 1837 by M. Jasevičius, recorded in Lithuanian folklore collections

name: Estonian Kannel
description: Estonia's plucked box zither, a small winged or trapezoid instrument of carved wood strung with wire or gut strings, played to accompany regilaul, the ancient runic-song tradition shared with Finland's kantele and Lithuania's kanklės. Regilaul texts and folk archaeology show the kannel in Baltic-Finnic music for over a millennium, and it remains central to Estonian folk revival ensembles.
material: carved wood, wire or gut strings
source: Estonian folk music scholarship; Estonian National Museum instrument collections
